blocks.text: It is proved that אפעה ephe is the viper.

Among the species of serpents, either truly or by repute, are: 1. אפעה ephe. 2. כפיר chephir. 3. עכשוב acsoub. 4. פתן pethen. 5. צבע tseboa. 6. צמאון tsimmaon. 7. צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni. 8. קפוז kippoz. 9. שחל sachal. 10. שפיפון sephiphon. 11. שרף saraph. 12. תנין thannin, which is also לויתן leviathan. The matter therefore requires that we speak of each one and try to distinguish these species from one another, although this is a very difficult thing, since in Scripture hardly anything is said of one species that is not common to all. Nor are the translators consistent. Still, I shall say what seems closest to the truth. In this chapter we shall deal with אפעה ephe, which is first in alphabetical order.

In the History of the Second Temple, p. 135, it is said of Cleopatra: וקראה להביאו [col. 358] לה אפעה והכנסתו תחת דדיה וישך אותה ותמת, And she ordered that אפעה ephe be brought to her; applied to her breasts, it killed her with its bite. Ephe, that is, the asp. For the common run of writers holds that Cleopatra was bitten by an asp. Strabo, book 17: Ἑαυτὴν ἐν τῇ φρουρᾷ διεχειρίσατο λάθρα δήγματι ἀσπίδος [Heautēn en tē phroura diecheirisato lathra dēgmati aspidos]; She secretly killed herself in custody by the bite of an asp. Velleius Paterculus, book 2: Cleopatra, having eluded her guards, had an asp brought in and, free of a woman's fear, gave up her breath at its bite. Suetonius in Augustus: She was thought to have died from the bite of an asp. Plutarch in Antony: Λέγεται δὲ τὴν ἀσπίδα κομισθῆναι σὺν τοῖς σύκοις [Legetai de tēn aspida komisthēnai syn tois sykois], etc. καὶ τὸν βραχίονα παρασχεῖν τῷ δήγματι γυμνώσασαν [kai ton brachiona paraschein tō dēgmati gymnōsasan]; [III, 126] They say that the asp was brought in with the figs, etc., and that she bared her arm and offered it to the bite. Again: Οἱ δὲ τηρεῖσθαι μὲν ἐν ὑδρίᾳ τὴν ἀσπίδα καθειργμένην φάσκουσιν [Hoi de tēreisthai men en hydria tēn aspida katheirgmenēn phaskousin]. Others say that the asp was kept shut up in a jar. [col. 359] And below: Οἷς ἔοικε πιστεύσας καὶ ὁ Καῖσαρ· ἐν γὰρ τῷ θριάμβῳ τῆς Κλεοπάτρας αὐτῆς εἴδωλον ἐκομίζετο, καὶ τῆς ἀσπίδος ἐμπεφυκυίας [Hois eoike pisteusas kai ho Kaisar; en gar tō thriambō tēs Kleopatras autēs eidōlon ekomizeto, kai tēs aspidos empephykuias]. Caesar seems to have believed them, since in the triumph an image of Cleopatra was carried, with asps fastened to it. Aelian, History, book 9, chapter 11: Τὸ τῆς ἀσπίδος δῆγμα πρᾳότατον εἶναι ἤλεγξε Κλεόπατρα [To tēs aspidos dēgma praotaton einai ēlenxe Kleopatra]; Cleopatra proved that the bite of the asp is the gentlest. And in chapter 61, after saying that the bite of the asp is scarcely detectable, because the poison lies hidden inside and is not spread over the surface: Ἔνθεν τοι καὶ τῆς Κλεοπάτρας ὁ θάνατος τοῖς ἀμφὶ τὸν Σεβαστὸν οὐ πάνυ τι ῥᾳδίως ἐγνώσθη [Enthen toi kai tēs Kleopatras ho thanatos tois amphi ton Sebaston ou pany ti rhadiōs egnōsthē]; Hence it is that the death of Cleopatra was not easily recognized by those around Augustus. Dio in Augustus: Ἀπέθανεν, ἀσπίδος αὐτῇ ἐν ὑδρίᾳ εἰσκομισθείσης [Apethanen, aspidos autē en hydria eiskomistheisēs]. She died, an asp having been brought to her in a jar. Galen, To Piso on Theriac, book 1, chapter 8, after treating the species of asps: Τούτων γοῦν φασι τῶν θηρίων τινὶ τὴν βασιλίδα Κλεοπάτραν, βουληθεῖσαν λαθεῖν τοὺς φυλάττοντας, ταχέως τε, καὶ ἀνυπόπτως ἀποθανεῖν [Toutōn goun phasi tōn thēriōn tini tēn basilida Kleopatran, boulētheisan lathein tous phylattontas, tacheōs te, kai anypoptōs apothanein]; They say, then, that by one of these beasts Queen Cleopatra, wishing to escape the notice of her guards, brought death on herself quickly and without suspicion. Tertullian, To the Martyrs, chapter 4: A woman willingly sought out beasts, and indeed asp serpents more horrid than a bull or a bear, which Cleopatra set upon herself so as not to fall into the hands of her enemy. Sextus Aurelius Victor, On Illustrious Men, under Cleopatra: When she pretended to bring funeral offerings to him (Antony) in his Mausoleum, she died by applying asps. Eutropius, book 7: Cleopatra let an asp at herself and was killed by its poison. Solinus: There are many different species of asps, but unequal in their effects for harm. The dipsas kills by thirst. The hypnale, because it kills by sleep, is bought for death, as Cleopatra also testifies. Isidore, Etymologies, book 12, chapter 4: The hypnalis, a kind of asp so called because it kills by sleep. This Cleopatra applied to herself, and so was released by death as if by sleep. Clearly, then, for the Hebrew writer אפעה ephe, which killed Cleopatra by its bite, is the asp. Likewise in Eutychius of Alexandria the same Cleopatra ordered those famous maidservants ان ياتياها بالافعا التي تسي بالاسغيدة [an yaʾtiyāhā bi-l-afʿā allatī tusī bi-l-asghīda] to bring her the ephe which they call the asp. For so one must read instead of the corrupt word بالاسيليدة [bi-l-asīlīda]. So in Iob. XX, 16. לשון אפעה, the tongue of the ephe, is in the Syriac ܠܫܢܐ ܕܐܣܦܣ, the tongue of the asp. And in Es. XXX, 6. the same version again has ܐܣܦܣ, asp, for אפעה ephe, and the Greeks ἀσπίδες [aspides].
